lesson.title: A Divided Peninsula, An Undeclared War: The Korean War
lesson.summary: When communist North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, the United States led a United Nations force to defend containment's credibility in Asia, fighting a brutal three-year war that ended not in victory but in a stalemate near where it began.
lesson.body:
Like Germany, Korea had been divided after World War II, split at the 38th parallel between a Soviet backed north and an American backed south, with the division originally intended as temporary. By 1950, two rival governments had formed: the communist Democratic People's Republic of Korea in the north, led by Kim Il-sung, and the Republic of Korea in the south, led by Syngman Rhee. Both governments claimed authority over the whole peninsula, and border skirmishes were common even before full scale war began.

On June 25, 1950, North Korean forces, with Soviet supplied weapons and Stalin's approval, invaded South Korea and quickly overran most of the peninsula. Because the Soviet Union happened to be boycotting the United Nations Security Council at the time over an unrelated dispute about which government should represent China, the Soviets were not present to veto a resolution authorizing a UN force to defend South Korea, a rare and consequential absence. The resulting UN force was overwhelmingly American, commanded by General Douglas MacArthur, and its intervention was a direct application of the containment strategy first outlined by Kennan and put into action through the Truman Doctrine, this time backed by American troops rather than just aid.

MacArthur staged a bold amphibious landing at Inchon in September 1950 that cut off North Korean forces and allowed UN troops to retake Seoul and push north, eventually approaching the Yalu River, the border with communist China. Alarmed by an American led army approaching its border, China entered the war in late October and November 1950, sending hundreds of thousands of troops that drove UN forces back south in a brutal winter retreat. The war then settled into a grinding stalemate roughly along the original 38th parallel, with both sides suffering enormous casualties for territory that changed hands repeatedly but ultimately shifted very little.

MacArthur publicly pushed for expanding the war into China itself, even suggesting the use of nuclear weapons, putting him at odds with Truman's more limited war aims and raising a fundamental question about civilian control of the military. Truman relieved MacArthur of command in April 1951, a controversial but constitutionally necessary assertion of presidential authority over the armed forces. Fighting dragged on for two more years of negotiations and limited offensives before an armistice was finally signed at Panmunjom on July 27, 1953, establishing a demilitarized zone near the original 38th parallel border. No side won a clear victory, and no formal peace treaty was ever signed; North and South Korea have technically remained in a state of armistice, rather than peace, ever since.
